rows.name: Qur'an
rows.detail: Tied to the verse of debt, 2:282 ('write it down'); Ibn Abbas held this verse was revealed regarding salam.
rows.detail_long: Who: The Qur'an is the first rung of every USUL ladder: it is never dated, and every later rung refers back to it. What: The longest verse in the Qur'an — the debt-documentation command — is salam's anchor by Ibn Abbas's occasion-of-revelation report: advance payment for deferred delivery is a debt, and debts are to be written. Why here: The Qur'an opens the Salam ladder and is never dated. Source: Qur'an 2:282.

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2240

topics_app: Sales in which a Price is paid for Goods to be Delivered Later (As-Salam)

rows.detail: 'Whoever pays in advance, let it be for a known measure, known weight, and a fixed term' — the clearest single contract hadith of all ten.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sahih al-Bukhari was compiled by Imam al-Bukhari (810-870), the most celebrated hadith scholar in Sunni Islam; it is widely regarded as the most authentic collection after the Qur'an. Narrator: Ibn Abbas. What: Ibn Abbas narrates: arriving at Medina, the Prophet found people prepaying for dates a year or two out, and regulated rather than banned it. The canonical exception to 'do not sell what you do not possess.' Practiced under Abu Bakr and Umar. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “The Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina and the people used to pay in advance the price of dates to be delivered within two or three years. He said (to them), "Whoever pays in advance the price of a thing to be delivered later should pay it for a specified measure at specified weight for a specified period." Hadart Ibn-u-Abi Najeeh said: Payment in advance should be for a specified measure for specified time.” It stands in Sales in which a Price is paid for Goods to be Delivered Later (As-Salam). Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Salam ladder; shown at 610 (no dated record; placed at the start of the Prophetic period (610)). Source: Sahih Bukhari 2240.

rows.name: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 1311
rows.detail: The Madinah salam rule, dated. On arriving in Madinah the Prophet finds advance-payment for fruit already in use and regulates it: known measure, known weight, specified period.
rows.detail_long: Who: Jami' al-Tirmidhi is the collection of Muhammad al-Tirmidhi (824-892), a scholar of the hadith sciences known as a master of hadith analysis. Narrator: Ibn Abbas. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library (Ibn Abbas): 'Whoever pays in advance, then let him pay in advance for known measurements, and known weights for a specified period of time.' Salam is not invented but STANDARDISED — the existing market practice is kept and given three mandatory specifications. Tirmidhi adds corroborating narrations from Ibn Abi Awfa and Abdur-Rahman bin Abza. The report (opening), as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Narrated Ibn 'Abbas: When the Prophet (ﷺ) arrived in Al-Madinah, they were paying in advance for fruits. So he said: 'Whoever pays in advance, then let him pay in advance for known measurements (of dates), and known weights for a specified period of time.' He said: There are narrations on this topic from Ibn Abi Awfa and 'Abdur-Rahman bin Abza. [Abu 'Eisa said:] The Hadith of Ibn 'Abbas is a Hasan Sahih Hadith. This is acted upon according to the people of knowledge among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and others. [...]” It stands in The Book on Business. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Salam ladder; shown at 622 (dated 622-700, low confidence; shown at the earliest year). Source: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 1311.

rows.name: Bulugh al-Maram 980
rows.detail: The pre-existing practice quantified: Madinans were paying one and two YEARS in advance for fruit when the specification rule came.
rows.detail_long: Who: Bulugh al-Maram is one of the hadith collections held in the Gold Ark Library. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: 'they were paying one and two years in advance for fruits. So he said: Those who paid in advance for fruits must do so for a specified measurement and weight, and for a specified time.' The tenor of the pre-Islamic forward market — multi-year — preserved inside the regulating hadith itself. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to al-Madinah, they were paying one and two years in advance for fruits. So he (ﷺ) said: "Those who paid in advance for fruits must do so for a specified measurement and weight, and for a specified time." .” It stands in Business Transactions. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Salam ladder; shown at 622 (dated 622-632 (Madinan period); shown at the earliest year). Source: Bulugh al-Maram 980.

rows.display_note: Companion dictum plus Malik's own doctrine in one record — fiqh forming inside the hadith corpus
rows.name: Muwatta 1397
rows.detail: Ibn Umar's salam conditions + Malik's refund rule. Ibn Umar: advance for food is fine with set description, price and date — but not in unripened crops. Malik adds: on failed delivery, take back exactly what you paid.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Muwatta is the work of Malik ibn Anas (711-795), the jurist of Medina and eponym of the Maliki school. Narrator: Nafi, from Abdullah ibn Umar. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: the companion rule (description + price + date, no advance on crops not yet ripening) and Malik's appended doctrine — if the seller cannot deliver at term and the sale is revoked, the buyer 'must only take back the silver, gold, or price which he paid exactly', and may not roll it into another purchase until repaid. The no-rollover rule protecting salam from mutating into disguised riba. The report (opening), as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Yahya related to me from Malik from Nafi that Abdullah ibn Umar said that there was no harm in a man making an advance to another man for food, with a set description and price until a set date, as long as it was not in crops, or dates which had not begun to ripen. [...]” It stands in Business Transactions. Why here: 'Companion practice' rung of the Salam ladder; shown at 622 (dated 622-632; shown at the earliest year). Source: Muwatta 1397.

rows.name: al-Tabari
rows.detail_long: Who: Abu Ja'far al-Tabari (839-923) was a Sunni scholar, historian, jurist and Qur'an commentator from Amol in Tabaristan who worked in Baghdad. He followed the Shafi'i school for nearly a decade, then developed his own school of law (the Jariri school), which lasted about two centuries after him. He is best known for his Qur'an commentary, Tafsir al-Tabari (Jami' al-Bayan), and his historical chronicle. What: Al-Tabari's enormous 2:282 treatment works the debt-documentation command clause by clause; the salam connection through Ibn Abbas's occasion-of-revelation report sits within it. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Salam ladder; shown at 923 (year of the author's death). Source: Jami' al-Bayan (Tafsir al-Tabari), on Q2:282.

rows.name: Malik ibn Anas
rows.detail: Treated as a distinct valid sale with strict conditions from Malik's Muwatta onward; all four schools follow.
rows.detail_long: Who: Malik ibn Anas (711-795), called the Imam of Medina, is the eponym of the Maliki school, one of the four Sunni schools of law; the school became the norm in much of North Africa and al-Andalus. Al-Muwatta is his work. Al-Shafi'i was his best-known student. What: From the Muwatta through al-Umm, al-Mabsut, Bada'i and al-Mughni, salam is a named contract with tight conditions — the schools differing mainly on whether goods must exist in the market between contract and delivery. In the work itself (vol. and page 2:644; our literal translation from the Arabic): “Yahya narrated to me, from Malik, from Nafi', from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, that he said: "There is no harm in the man paying the man in advance for described food at a known price to a named term, so long as it is not in a crop whose soundness has not appeared, or dates whose soundness has not appeared."” It also states: “[Malik, on one who paid in advance for food and at the term the seller could not deliver:] and he released him [from the sale]; then it is not fitting for him to take from him except his silver or his gold or the very price that he paid to him.” It also states: “Malik said: and the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, forbade the sale of food before it is taken in full.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Salam ladder, Maliki voice; shown at 795 (year of the author's death). Source: Al-Muwatta.

rows.name: al-Quduri
rows.detail: Al-Quduri permits salam in goods that are dry-measured, weighed, counted and regular, or measured by length; not in animals.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Quduri (362-428 AH) was a jurist of the Hanafi school; his Mukhtasar is the classic Hanafi primer. What: The classic Hanafi primer lists where salam is permitted and where it is not (animals and their parts, numbered hides, bundled firewood and similar). Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Salam ladder, Hanafi voice; shown at 1037 (428 AH (death) as printed on the translation's title page; CE year by calendar conversion (428 AH = 1036-37 CE)). Source: Mukhtasar al-Quduri, chapter on Salam.

rows.name: Yahya ibn Sharif al-Nawawi
rows.detail: Al-Nawawi: 'The salam or advance is a sale of goods that have not been seen, but are specified in the contract.'
rows.detail_long: Who: Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Nawawi (1233-1277), known as Muhyi al-Din, was a Shafi'i jurist and hadith scholar of Damascus. His works include Minhaj al-Talibin and Riyad al-Salihin; al-Asnawi described him as the editor and refiner of the Shafi'i school. What: The standard Shafi'i manual defines salam as a sale by description. Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Salam ladder, Shafi'i voice; shown at 1277 (year of the author's death). Source: Minhaj al-Talibin, Book 10 (Sale by Advance).

rows.name: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi
rows.detail: Ibn Qudama: 'Advance payment is valid for everything that matches the description exactly', with quantity stated, a delivery date fixed and the price paid before the parties separate.
rows.detail_long: Who: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi (1147-1223) was a jurist of the Hanbali school who studied in Baghdad and taught in Damascus; he is regarded as one of the school's most authoritative classical figures. He is best known for al-Mughni, a legal encyclopedia that compares the opinions of the Sunni schools while setting out the Hanbali position in detail. He also wrote 'Umdat al-Fiqh. What: The Hanbali primer sets the conditions of salam: precise description, stated quantity, fixed delivery date, price paid at the session. Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Salam ladder, Hanbali voice; shown at 1223 (year of the author's death). Source: 'Umdat al-Fiqh, chapter on Advance Payment (al-Salam).

rows.name: AAOIFI
rows.detail: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 10 (Salam and Parallel Salam); salam sukuk issued by Bahrain and The Gambia.
rows.detail_long: Who: AAOIFI (the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions) issues the Shari'ah Standards. They are mandatory in Bahrain, its home jurisdiction, and adopted in the UAE and other countries. What: SS10 codifies salam and back-to-back parallel salam for commodity and treasury use. Rules adopted 23 May 2001, reformatted as Standard 16 May 2002. Clauses read in the standard's text: 3/1/1 salam capital may be fungible goods provided no riba arises; 3/2/1 salam is for fungibles that can be weighed, measured or counted; 4/1 the buyer may NOT sell al-muslam fihi before taking possession; 5/1 the seller must deliver on the due date per agreed specification and quantity; 6/1 parallel salam with a third party is permitted only as a separate, independent contract. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Salam ladder; shown at 2002 (adopted as rules 19-23 May 2001 (meeting 6); readopted as a Standard at meeting 8, 11-16 May 2002). Source: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 10 (Salam and Parallel Salam); salam sukuk issued by Bahrain and The Gambia.
